topic: The Magic of the Central Limit Theorem: Finding Order in Chaos
target_audience: University students or high school students with basic statistics knowledge

sections.title: The Mystery of Chaos
lecture_lines: The world is often messy and unpredictable.
Individual data points can appear completely random.
Can we find order within this chaotic data?
animations: Fade in title "The Mystery of Chaos" in light blue (#ADD8E6) at the top.
Display a chaotic scatter plot of dots with random sizes in yellow (#FFFF00).
Flash extreme dots in red (#FF0000) to show data variability.
Show a white (#FFFFFF) pulsing question mark [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/question.svg] in the center of the chaos.
Transition dots into a skewed green (#00FF00) population bar chart.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Building Blocks
lecture_lines: Every population has a mean and standard deviation.
A distribution shows how often different values occur.
Our "Chaos Island" monsters have a flat distribution.
animations: Display a flat cyan (#00FFFF) rectangular bar chart representing a uniform distribution of monsters [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/monsters.svg].
Draw a vertical orange (#FFA500) line in the center labeled population mean mu.
Use magenta (#FF00FF) arrows to indicate standard deviation sigma from the center.

sections.title: The Sampling Experiment
lecture_lines: Let's take random groups, or samples, of monsters.
For each group, we calculate the average weight.
This average is called the "Sample Mean."
We repeat this process many, many times.
Each sample gives us one new data point.
animations: Show a group of 30 monster [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/monster.svg] icons flickering in lime (#32CD32) to represent sampling.
Display the sample mean formula X-bar in gold (#FFD700) above the group.
Populate a white (#FFFFFF) list with multiple sample mean values like X1, X2...

sections.title: The Visual Transformation
lecture_lines: Watch the distribution of these sample means change.
Initially, the averages might look a bit scattered.
As we collect more samples, a pattern emerges.
The messy distribution morphs into a smooth curve.
It becomes the famous, symmetrical Bell Curve.
animations: Show the original messy rectangular histogram dimmed in the background.
Plot new sample mean points in yellow (#FFFF00) along the horizontal axis.
Morph the accumulating points into a rough light blue (#ADD8E6) bell shape.
Smooth the rough shape into a perfect pink (#FFC0CB) normal distribution curve.
Flash the final curve to emphasize the completed transformation.

sections.title: The Core Theorem (The Magic Rule)
lecture_lines: This is the Central Limit Theorem in action.
The center stays at the true population mean.
Increasing sample size makes the curve much narrower.
With enough samples, the shape is always Normal.
Chaos transforms into predictable, mathematical order.
animations: Display the formula X-bar ~ N(mu, sigma squared over n) in white (#FFFFFF).
Draw a wide green (#00FF00) bell curve representing a small sample size.
Animate an 'n' value increasing to show larger sample groups.
Squeeze the green bell curve to make it taller and narrower.
Highlight the constant center line mu in red (#FF0000).

sections.title: Real-World Application
lecture_lines: The CLT is the foundation of modern statistics.
We can predict populations from just a few samples.
Science and industry rely on this mathematical magic.
animations: Display silver (#C0C0C0) battery [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/battery.svg] icons to represent a large factory [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/factory.svg] production.
Contrast the total population N with a small sample group n=30 in yellow (#FFFF00).
Draw a green (#00FF00) bell curve to represent the predictable quality confidence.
